paper_title: R$^2$Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R$^2$Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R$^2$Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: In recent years, variety of powerful agentic systems have been applied to solve wide range of human problems (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c), gradually moving beyond hand-written agent pipelines toward orchestrators that learn to compose agent teams. In this process, the agent graph has become key bridge from task goals to executable collaboration: by giving each node role and each edge hand-off, orchestrators solve tasks with improved 1 Figure 1: recursion needs two channels: the outer loop sets the inner loops objective, and the inner loop, ProposerDirector self-play on randomized rollout group, returns the evidence for withdrawing skills. controllability, compositionality, and reusability (Zhang et al., 2025, 2026c), as shown in Figure 1. However, in practice, orchestrators still learn from tasks people collect and lean on in-prompt skills (Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d), making them costly to scale and hard to improve on their own. To address these issues, three main lines of work have emerged, as shown in Figure 2. First, learned orchestration optimizes workflows and planning from task feedback (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c), taking the task pool as given. Second, self-improving agents refine their own memory, harness code, answers, or tasks through repeated loops (Zhu et al., 2026; Srikanth et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Lu et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026). Third, skill scaffolds hand procedural knowledge to policy (Zhang et al., 2026d; Shi et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b; Shen et al., 2026), in context at inference or as training-time support. However, these methods still face three challenges (Figure 2ac). (i) Hand-designed curricula. Learned orchestration and skill internalization practice on task pools that people collect in advance Figure 2: Paradigm comparison. (a) Learned orchestration trains on hand-designed static curriculum. (b) Selfimproving agents measure the frontier with skills present, skill-anchored frontier where advantages collapse once skills leave. (c) Skill scaffolds withdraw guidance through success-rate gates, unreliable evaluation signals pinned by self-play. (d) R2Orch nests two loops joined by downward (objective) and upward (evidence) channels. (Zhang et al., 2026c; Shi et al., 2026), and self-play chooses its own tasks while the solver keeps retrieving its skills (Fu et al., 2026), so choosing tasks and withdrawing skills do not inform each other. (ii) Advantage collapse. Group-based RL such as GRPO learns from differences among tasks rollouts, which vanish when they all reach the same outcome (He et al., 2026); self-play keeps tasks at the solvers frontier with skills in context (Fu et al., 2026), so withdrawing skill pushes the tasks it supported toward all-wrong rollouts, and advantage collapse returns. (iii) Unreliable evaluation signals. Training-time scaffolds fade guidance on success rate mixing task choice with the skills effect (Shi et al., 2026), and skill libraries keep or retire skills on one noisy score each, so they drift until injecting skill scores worse than injecting nothing (Zhang et al., 2026e; Zhang et al.). To address these challenges, we propose R2Orch (Fig. 2d), new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration, in which an inner loop of self-play improves the orchestrator, Director, on tasks Proposer chooses, and an outer loop improves how the inner loop improves. Two channels join the loops, one carrying the objective down and one the evidence up. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, the downward channel, which rewards the Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn, scoring each task with the candidate skill withheld. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, the upward channel, in which random part of each rollout group hides one skill, turning self-play into controlled evaluation whose Bayesian posterior over the skills remaining benefit decides when it can leave. The two loops thus close into one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the Director improves on its own and moves toward zero-skill deployment. We evaluate R2Orch on twelve benchmarks in question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. Results show that R2Orch outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, improves six other Worker backbones without retraining, and keeps its accuracy when tested with zero skills. Together, these results mark step toward the recursive selfimprovement of agent orchestrators.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Learned Orchestration and Self-Play. Prior work searches agent workflows (Zhang et al., 2025), learns graph editing (Zhang et al., 2026c), or trains the planner of an agent system (Li et al., 2026), over tasks that people collect in advance. Self-play lets Proposer pose tasks to solver, rewarding regret (Dennis et al., 2020), solver uncertainty (Huang et al., 2026), or learning progress while distilling failures into skills (Fu et al., 2026). Group-based RL (Shao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) gives no advantage to task whose rollouts all reach the same outcome (He et al., 2026), so curricula favor learnable tasks (Rutherford et al., 2024) or filter the rest out (Yu et al., 2026). R2Orch scores tasks with the candidate skill withheld, so its Proposer picks tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes instead of filtering collapsed ones. Skill Evolution and Self-Improvement. Skills enter the prompt at inference (Zhang et al., 2026d) or support training and are withdrawn on success2 rate threshold (Shi et al., 2026), preset budget (Lu et al., 2026b), or leave-one-skill-out validation (Shen et al., 2026). Rollouts with and without skill score it (Tu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), paired tests accept self-modifications (Shawn, 2026), and one noisy score per skill lets library drift (Zhang et al., 2026e). Recursive self-improvement systems revise their own memory, code, or answers (Zhu et al., 2026; Srikanth et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026) or adopt self-modification once it is shown to help (Schmidhuber, 2007; Zhang et al., 2026a). R2Orch nests self-play in skillwithdrawal loop and decides each withdrawal from the controlled evaluation within every randomized rollout group, at no extra rollouts.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate R2Orch through the following research questions (RQs). RQ1: How does R2Orch compare with the baselines in distribution and on heldout benchmarks? RQ2: Does the trained Director transfer to other Worker backbones without retraining? RQ3: Do both loops of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration contribute, and does the Director keep its accuracy at zero skills (Section 4.1)? RQ4: Does Recursive Learnability choose the tasks that keep yielding learning signal as skills are withdrawn (Section 4.2)? RQ5: Does Skill Withdrawal remove each skill only once the Director no longer needs it (Section 4.3)? Setup. Six in-distribution (IID) benchmarks supply the training tasks and IID tests, and six out-ofdistribution (OOD) benchmarks are held out. The baselines span direct prompting, backbone training, workflow search, RL-trained orchestration, skill internalization, and self-play with skill evolution, under the shared protocol of Table 1 (Appendix D). Main results (RQ1). R2Orch is best on all twelve benchmarks against six families of baselines, and its lead holds on the held-out half at zero skills  (Table 1)  . Training the backbone alone changes little, while orchestration lifts the frozen Workers far higher, so the gains come from how the Workers are organized. The other orchestrators learn from signals that stop tracking the Director: fixed task pools (workflow search, RL-trained orchestration), success rates or budgets (skill internalization), and frontiers measured with skills in context (self-play). R2Orch replaces these signals with Recursive Learnability and Skill Withdrawal, so its lead is largest on AIME 2026, WebShop, and ALFWorld, where the ablations cost most  (Table 2)  . Backbone transfer (RQ2). The Director trained with Qwen3.5-9B Workers improves all six other backbones on every benchmark without retraining (Figure 4e), since the roles and hand-offs it builds fit any Worker. Weaker backbones gain the most, narrowing the IID range across backbones from 25.7 to 6.4 points, because the graph supplies the planning and checking they lack. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: R2Orch nests two loops: Recursive Learnability picks tasks learnable without the candidate skill, and Skill Withdrawal retires skills that stop helping. It leads on all twelve benchmarks at zero skills.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: R2Orch starts from initial skills that we customize by hand for each dataset, and the withdrawals, revisions, and distillations that follow build on them, so deriving the initial skills automatically for new domain remains an open problem.

sections.title: Ethical considerations
sections.content: R2Orch is trained and evaluated on public benchmarks that we use for research evaluation as their creators intend, and the study involves no human participants, annotators, or personal data. ALFWorld and WebShop are simulated environments, and the code benchmarks run in their standard evaluation harnesses. Agents that orchestrate tools can be misused like any agent system, and selfimproving orchestrator shares this risk, so we release the code for inspection and recommend running it in sandboxed environment.
